How to read this document

Every quantitative claim carries a provenance label. The distinction is the point of the document, not decoration:

Measured observed in a live run against a real provider   Estimated extrapolated from a small sample  
Mocked verified by tests that never contact a provider   Unverified designed and reasoned, not demonstrated

The single most important caveat

Answer quality has never been evaluated. The router's central premise — that a cheap model is good enough for prompts classified "simple" — has no eval behind it. Every cost and latency figure in this document is real; none of them say the answers were correct.

1 · Executive summary

Problem

The platform's original design queried every configured model for every prompt. Cost scales as O(models × prompts), and most of that spend goes to the most expensive model even when the prompt does not need its capability.

The obvious fix — call the cheap model first, ask how confident it is, escalate if unsure — fails twice:

  • Latency. Every escalation pays small-model latency plus large-model latency sequentially. Tail latency becomes worse than simply calling the large model.
  • Signal quality. Small models are confidently wrong, so self-reported confidence is close to the least reliable escalation signal available.

Goals

GoalRoute most prompts to a low-cost model without materially degrading quality.
GoalNever make an LLM call whose only purpose is deciding whether to make another LLM call.
GoalEscalate on objective, externally observable signals — not self-rating.
GoalReport savings against a measured baseline, not a token-count estimate.
Non-goalGuaranteeing the cheap tier never underperforms. The router reduces that rate; it does not eliminate it.
Non-goalReplacing side-by-side comparison mode. The router is a separate, opt-in path.

Approach

Two decision stages run before any model is called — deterministic regex heuristics, then a local logistic-regression classifier over a hashed text embedding. Neither touches the network. A prompt that was always going to need the large model goes there directly, which keeps the double-latency path a minority of traffic rather than the default.

Two numbers that must carry their caveats

The saving is an estimate. The baseline is extrapolated from four shadow-sampled requests across 116 fast-path requests. The direction is sound; the precision is not. Read it as "roughly 40%", never 39.1%, and not as a statistically robust or universally applicable figure.

The fast-path share is 52%, not 74.8%. The dashboard shows 74.8% because the 155 logged requests include three deliberate repeat passes over the 30 simple prompts, run to make 5% shadow sampling fire at all. Over the distinct 60-prompt corpus it is 52% — the figure used throughout this document.

2 · Architecture and routing decision flow

Two independent paths over one shared provider layer. The router is opt-in and does not replace comparison mode.

prompt │ ├─ Stage 1 · regex heuristics local, ~0 ms, free │ code fence · "step by step" · math operators │ match ────────────────────────────────────────────────► TIER 2 │ no match │ ├─ Stage 2 · logistic regression local, 0.07 ms warm │ over FNV-1a hashed embedding, 512-dim │ complex │ cold start ─────────────────────────────────► TIER 2 │ simple │ ├─ TIER 1 · gpt-4o-mini │ ├─ Escalation gate · objective signals, cheapest first │ 1. schema / format invalid free ──► constrained repair, then TIER 2 │ 2. mean token logprob < τ free ──────────────────► TIER 2 │ 3. two samples disagree +1 call ──────────────────► TIER 2 │ (only when logprobs unavailable) │ └─ Request logger · one row per request, on every path
The constraint that shapes everything

No LLM call is ever made whose only purpose is deciding whether to make another LLM call. Both pre-query stages are local, so routing adds no network tax to any request. A router that called a model to classify complexity would reintroduce the exact cost and latency problem it exists to solve.

Why the escalation signals are what they are

SignalApplies whenMarginal cost
Schema / format validationOutput shape is declaredfree
Token logprob below τProvider exposes logprobsfree — same response
Self-consistencyLogprobs unavailable+1 Tier 1 call

Checked cheapest-first. The paid signal runs only when the free ones cannot decide — a property that is invisible in output and is therefore asserted directly by a test (§5).

These are verbatim extracts from the Claude Code session transcript for this project (22 prompts, 16 Sept – 13 Oct 2026). Trims are marked […]; nothing is paraphrased. Claude Code wrote most of the implementation; I set the constraints, rejected output that did not survive checking, and verified every claim against artifacts before accepting it.

Decision points that changed the design

DecisionAlternative rejectedWhy

A full iteration: initial approach → failure → revision → test

The problem was framed by supplying a complete 13,370-character architecture specification — problem statement, goals and non-goals, two-stage classification, the escalation signals, benchmarking strategy, metrics, design decisions, open questions and a log schema. The reasoning quoted in §1 and §2 of this document originates there, not from the model. 2 · Evidence — 17 Sept, 06:10 (quoted in full)
"Run 50–100 real prompts through /router
Mix easy and hard ones so both tiers and the escalation gate actually fire."

Three findings, none visible offline. (a) gpt-4 is listed by /v1/models but returns 404 to project-scoped keys — 29 of 60 calls failed. (b) No retry existed for 429, and a 3 requests/minute cap silently lost 4 of 60 prompts. (c) All 8 escalations were schema failures, and the expensive model did not fix them (§4).

Prefer structured outputs or a bounded constrained retry for formatting failures, where supported. / Avoid infinite retry loops and duplicate requests. / Implement or verify bounded exponential backoff for OpenAI 429 responses, respecting Retry-After when provided. / Preserve useful error reporting and ensure failed requests are accounted for accurately. / Keep the implementation consistent with the existing architecture."
4 · Verification — same message (quoted in full)
"Run the existing tests, typecheck, and lint. Add regression tests for any changes, particularly schema recovery and rate-limit handling. Use mocks for failure scenarios rather than spending API credits unnecessarily.

Do not claim that live API behavior has been tested unless you actually tested it. Do not change expected behavior merely to make tests pass."

Result. 109 → 136 tests. The new suite immediately caught a defect in the retry code itself (§5). Tests, typecheck, lint and build all pass.

The standing instruction that shaped the work

"Work incrementally. Inspect before editing. Preserve the existing design and working features. Do not rewrite the whole application, change model providers unnecessarily, or run the full live corpus without asking me first." — 13 Oct, 10:08, quoted in full.

How I directed and checked the AI

  • Constraints before code. "Never make an LLM call to decide whether to make an LLM call" ruled out an entire class of design before any was written.
  • Ran it, did not just build it. Typecheck and build both passed while a duplicate provider map made a model unreachable from one endpoint. Only driving the running app exposed it.
  • Checked claims against artifacts. Test counts here come from the JSON reporter; live figures were recomputed from .data/requests.jsonl, not copied from an earlier summary.
  • Rejected a plausible recommendation. Claude Code proposed Claude Haiku → Opus on a "5× price spread" argument. The arithmetic showed that pairing roughly halves projected savings: Anthropic exposes no logprobs, so every gate check would fall through to the paid self-consistency signal. The tiers stayed on OpenAI.
  • Corrected the AI's own draft claims. Draft CV text it generated said the router "eliminates" the double-latency penalty. It does not — escalated prompts still pay both latencies; the design confines that path to a minority. Corrected to "avoids for pre-classified prompts".

4 · Live findings and the schema-failure case study

Case study — escalation was the wrong remedy

Observation. Across 155 live requests, all 8 escalations were schema_fail. Not one was triggered by the logprob gate.

Why the logprob gate never fired — threshold, not wiring

The request log stores no logprob values, so this was established indirectly. Logprobs were requested and returned: Tier 1 is an OpenAI model, wantLogprobs is set for it, and a direct probe confirmed gpt-4o-mini returns them. Decisively, had they been absent the gate would have fallen through to self-consistency on every fast-path request — doubling the Tier 1 calls. It did not: 0 of 116 fast-path rows show doubled token counts (median tokens_in = 15, max 25), and there are 0 inconsistent escalations. So the values were present, read, and simply never fell below τ = −1.0. The threshold is uncalibrated for this model and workload, not broken. It has been left unchanged pending calibration against real logprob distributions.

Probe. Asked for a two-letter ISO country code under the schema ^[A-Z]{2}$, Tier 1 returned prose. The request escalated to gpt-4o, which returned:

The ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code for Norway is "NO".

Also prose. Also a schema violation. The router had paid the expensive tier to reproduce the same failure.

Diagnosis

A formatting miss is not a capability gap. The design had assumed one remedy — escalate — for all three signals, and that assumption was wrong for the signal that turned out to fire most. A larger model is the right answer to "this model isn't smart enough" and the wrong answer to "this model didn't follow the output contract".

The fix: remedy chosen by cause

Tripped signalRemedy nowRationale
logprob_lowEscalate to Tier 2Low confidence is a capability gap.
inconsistentEscalate to Tier 2Sample disagreement likewise suggests the task exceeds the tier.
schema_failOne bounded constrained retry at Tier 1, then escalate if still failingAddresses the actual cause on the tier whose list price is 16.7× lower (gpt-4o : gpt-4o-mini list ratio, not a measured per-request saving).

The repair restates the constraint as a system instruction, runs at temperature 0, and sets response_format: json_object where the model supports it. It is bounded by SCHEMA_REPAIR_ATTEMPTS (default 1) so a model that cannot satisfy a schema cannot drive unbounded spend. The outcome is recorded in a new schema_repaired log field.

What is not yet known about this fix

Its control flow is covered by mocked tests. Its live success rate is unmeasured. Whether a real model obeys the repair instruction often enough to beat escalating is reasoned, not demonstrated. The field exists precisely so that becomes measurable — and schema_repaired appears in 0 of the 155 logged rows, because that data predates the change.

The other two live findings

A model that is listed but not callable

gpt-4 appears in GET /v1/models for this account yet returns 404 — does not exist or you do not have access to a project-scoped (sk-proj-…) key whose allowlist excludes it. The org-level list overstates what a given key can call. Tiers were then selected by probing the key directly: gpt-4o-mini → gpt-4o, a 16.7× spread with logprobs available on both.

No retry on rate limits

The account is capped at 3 requests/minute on gpt-4o; the raw-fetch adapters had no retry at all, so 4 of 60 prompts simply failed. They now retry with bounded backoff: at most 3 attempts, Retry-After honoured as delta-seconds or HTTP date, otherwise exponential backoff with jitter, both capped at 30 s.

A deliberate decision: timeouts are not retried

Only explicit 429 and 5xx responses are retried; network errors and timeouts are not. A timed-out request may have been received and billed, so repeating it risks a duplicate charge and a duplicate completion. A 429 is an outright rejection, so a repeat is safe. A 5xx usually means the work was not done, but that is not guaranteed — which is why the 3-attempt bound matters: it caps the duplicate-charge exposure rather than eliminating it.

5 · Testing strategy

136 tests, 10 files, roughly 250 ms, entirely offline. API keys are blanked in vitest.config.mts, so a test that reaches a provider is a failing test.

FileTestsLayerWhat it covers
heuristics21UnitEvery Stage 1 rule in both directions — over-matching forfeits savings, under-matching sends hard prompts to the weak tier.
embedding10UnitDeterminism, L2 normalisation, zero-vector on empty input, stable embedder id (the trained weights are bound to it).
classifier8UnitSigmoid overflow bounds, monotonicity, cold-start reporting, provenance.
escalation20Unit + behaviouralEach signal, plus signal ordering — asserted with a spy that fails if the paid resample is reached.
pricing7UnitCost arithmetic, linearity, and the invariant that Tier 1 is strictly cheaper than Tier 2.
metrics21UnitPercentile edges and honesty properties: no baseline without a sample, null not zero on an empty log, negative savings surfaced not hidden.
retry14UnitRetry-After as seconds and as HTTP date, caps, jitter, bounded worst case.
router14IntegrationDecision → correct model called; every caused call billed; one log row per path; field set checked against the design document.
repair13IntegrationFull repair flow: success avoids Tier 2, failure escalates, boundedness, and the three cases where repair must not fire.
routing.golden8Golden outputAggregate routing across all 60 corpus prompts pinned to {31, 15, 14}; known-misroute tracking; Stage 2 latency budget.

How the layers fit together

Each layer exists because the one below it cannot see a particular class of defect:

  • Unit tests catch rule errors in isolation, but cannot see cost.
  • Behavioural tests catch regressions that produce identical output and cost more. Verified by mutation: removing the gate's short-circuit on healthy logprobs changes no response and doubles fast-path cost — four tests across two files fail.
  • Golden output pins the aggregate routing distribution, because cost follows directly from those three numbers. A drift in routing is a drift in the savings claim.
  • Integration tests catch wiring the others cannot see — that a decision actually reaches the right model and that every call made is billed.
  • Running the application remains its own layer. A duplicate provider map passed typecheck, lint and build, and was caught only by driving the live app.
Known defects are tracked, not hidden

The golden test holds a KNOWN_MISROUTES map of five prompts the classifier routes against intent, with a diagnosed cause: every complex training example opens with an imperative verb, so the model learned "imperative ⇒ complex" and trips on Return, List, Fix. Holdout accuracy of 86.7% did not surface this; running the corpus did. The map is deliberately not a relabelling — the test fails on a new misroute and also when one is fixed.

What each gate has actually caught

GateReal defect
Running the appDuplicate provider map made claude-opus-5 unreachable from one endpoint while the router handled it. Typecheck and build both passed.
Live API runThree defects invisible offline: gpt-4 listed but 404 for project-scoped keys (29 of 60 calls failed); no 429 retry (4 of 60 lost); escalation does not repair schema failures (§4).
npm testA negative Retry-After fell through to Date.parse("-5"), which succeeds as a past date, yielding a 0 ms delay — a hot-retry loop.
npm testA test asserted p50 of [100,120] was 120; nearest-rank makes it 100. The test was wrong, the code was right.
tscA type error in a test file that passed at runtime — Vitest does not typecheck.
next lintAn unused parameter introduced by the fix for that.

6 · What was not tested, and accepted risks

Ordered by how much each would matter in production.

Not coveredRisk acceptedStatus
Answer quality at either tier The router's core premise has no eval behind it. Nothing verifies that the cheap tier is good enough, or that escalating yields a better answer. The largest accepted risk in the project. Unverified
Schema repair on live traffic Control flow is covered by mocked tests; the real hit rate is unknown, so "cheaper than escalating" is reasoned, not demonstrated. Unverified
Retry policy against a live 429 Unit-tested only. Reproducing a real rate limit means deliberately burning quota, so the policy has not been re-validated end to end since the failure that motivated it. Unverified
Provider adapters against real APIs No recorded fixtures. A provider changing its response shape breaks parsing and no test catches it; mitigated only by the adapters being thin and failing loudly. Unverified
Anthropic adapter end to end Never exercised with a live key. Its retry comes from the official SDK rather than the shared helper, so the two providers have different retry semantics — deliberate, but not uniform and not tested. Unverified
Concurrency and load Single-request paths only. The retry jitter's purpose — desynchronising concurrent callers — is therefore unproven. Unverified
The request log stores no model outputs Only routing, tokens, cost and latency are recorded. Cost and latency are therefore auditable after the fact; answer quality is not. A retrospective quality spot-check over the 155 logged requests is impossible without re-running them and paying again — a direct consequence of the schema choice, and the first thing to change. Unverified
React pages Exercised by hand against the running app; no component tests. Unverified
Request log on a serverless filesystem Append-only JSONL assumes a persistent disk. A serverless deployment needs a real datastore; the read/write pair is the only surface that would change. Unverified
Pricing accuracy Anthropic rates came from a published table; OpenAI and Google rates are hand-entered and unchecked. Tests confirm the arithmetic, never the inputs — every dollar figure inherits this caveat. Unverified
Classifier beyond the corpus 86.7% holdout on 149 examples, below the 200–500 the design targets, with 100% train accuracy indicating overfitting. Five misroutes tracked. Measured

Standing assumptions that remain unverified

  • That prompts the classifier labels "simple" genuinely are simple enough for the cheap tier — the premise the whole cost argument rests on.
  • That a 5% shadow sample represents the fast-path population. Four samples is far too few to support that; the figure is a direction, not a result.
  • That the 60-prompt corpus resembles real traffic. It was hand-written, so the 52% fast-path share is a property of the corpus, not of production.
  • That hand-written heuristics will not go stale or be gamed as prompt patterns shift.

7 · Outcomes, lessons, and next steps

What the project demonstrates

  • A working two-tier router whose pre-query stages make no network call, measured at 0.07 ms warm.
  • A measured cost reduction of roughly 40% on a real workload, reported with its sample size and its label attached rather than rounded into a headline.
  • Latency separated by routing path, showing the escalated path genuinely is slower (1499 ms p50 against 856 ms) and genuinely is a minority (6.5%) — which is precisely the design's claim.
  • An observability pipeline built so the baseline is collected rather than assumed, including the deliberate cost of shadow sampling.
  • 136 offline tests across four layers, with a mutation check proving the suite catches cost-only regressions.

Lessons

  1. Offline checks certify structure, not behaviour. Typecheck, lint, build and 109 tests all passed while a model was unreachable from one endpoint and the retry path did not exist. Every finding that changed the design came from running the thing.
  2. An aggregate metric can conceal a systematic fault. 86.7% holdout accuracy looked healthy; running the corpus exposed five misroutes sharing one diagnosable cause.
  3. Match the remedy to the cause. The design applied one remedy to three signals. For the signal that fired most, that remedy cost 17× and fixed nothing.
  4. A plausible recommendation is not a verified one. The Claude-tier proposal was well argued and wrong once the arithmetic included the self-consistency tax.
  5. Measurement needs designing in. Had shadow sampling not been built up front, there would be no baseline now — only an estimate derived from token counts, which is exactly what the design set out to avoid.

What I would do next, and why

Next stepWhy it comes first
1. Build a quality evalEvery cost claim is currently unanchored. A router that saves 40% while degrading answers is a worse product, and nothing in the project would currently detect that. This is the gap that most limits what the measured results mean.
2. Measure the repair hit rateThe field exists and logs nothing yet. A few hundred live requests would turn "reasoned" into "measured" and settle whether repair genuinely beats escalation.
3. Raise shadow samples into double figuresFour samples cannot support a precise savings figure. More volume — or a temporarily raised sample rate for a deliberate measurement run — would narrow the uncertainty.
4. Expand and rebalance the training set149 examples with every complex case opening on an imperative produced a diagnosable bias. Targeted counter-examples should remove the five known misroutes.
5. Log model outputsWithout them no quality claim can ever be checked retrospectively, and step 1 cannot be done on existing traffic. Cheap to add; unblocks everything about quality.
6. Calibrate τ against real logprob distributionsThe gate has never fired, so the threshold is currently decorative.
7. Verify the pricing tableCheap to do, and every dollar figure depends on it.
8. Recorded fixtures for provider adaptersWould catch a provider changing response shape without needing live keys in CI.
9. Replace the JSONL log for deploymentRequired before any serverless deployment; the interface is already narrow enough to swap.

8 · Demo and repository

Repository

github.com/Ghasanjaber/LLM-Evaluation-Platform

Status of the repository at the time of writing

The remote contains the router, the corpus, the design document and the dashboard. The work described in §4 and §5 — the test suite, the schema-repair path, the retry policy and the submission documentation — was complete and verified locally but not yet committed or pushed when this document was generated. Confirm the push before submitting, or the reviewer will not see the test suite.

Reproducing the offline demo — no API key, no spend

git clone https://github.com/Ghasanjaber/LLM-Evaluation-Platform.git
cd LLM-Evaluation-Platform
npm install
npm run train:classifier     # fits the Stage 2 classifier from the seed set

npm test                     # 136 tests, ~250 ms, fully offline
npm run corpus               # routing over 60 prompts; prints the 5 tracked misroutes

Reproducing the live demo

cp .env.example .env.local   # add OPENAI_API_KEY
npm run dev                  # terminal 1
npm run corpus -- --live     # terminal 2 — about $0.03, ~5 min at 3 RPM

Then at http://localhost:3000/router:

PromptExpected path
What is the capital of Norway?Tier 1 fast path
Write a function that reverses a listStage 1 → Tier 2; Tier 1 never called
Give the ISO code for Norway (regex ^[A-Z]{2}$)Schema failure → constrained repair → repaired or escalated

Requires Node 18+ (developed on Node 24). OPENAI_API_KEY is the only key the router needs; both tiers are OpenAI models.

No recorded video demo is included
